assessments.title: Entrepreneurship Main Contest: Week 1 - Customer discovery - day4-slot1
assessments.description: Original main contest assessment on customer discovery. Case: Umoja Print Corner is exploring short-run print orders for student associations, after a schedule change. Distinguish recorded facts from assumptions and judge each decision against the case.
learning_objectives: Apply customer discovery principles to the Umoja Print Corner case.
Distinguish observed information from an unverified assumption.
Choose a proportionate next action and explain its tradeoffs.

questions.prompt: Which opening question best learns how student associations handle approving a proof?
options: Would you pay for the feature we designed?
You agree this is a serious problem, don't you?
Tell me about the last time you handled it and what happened next.
You would use our proposed service, right?
questions.correct_answer: Tell me about the last time you handled it and what happened next.
questions.rationale: A recent episode invites concrete recall without steering the answer toward a proposed solution.

questions.prompt: Which note is an observation from a discovery conversation?
options: A reminder feature will solve the problem.
The customer described calling three providers after two messages went unanswered.
The customer is careless about planning.
Everyone in this group needs an app.
questions.correct_answer: The customer described calling three providers after two messages went unanswered.
questions.rationale: The reported calls and unanswered messages describe an account; judgments about motive or solution are inferences.

questions.prompt: One interviewee describes a painful delay. What can the founder conclude? In this case, the team is working after a schedule change; keep that constraint in view.
options: This account suggests a hypothesis to investigate with other relevant customers.
The whole market has the same problem.
The interviewee will buy the proposed product.
The proposed product is already validated.
questions.correct_answer: This account suggests a hypothesis to investigate with other relevant customers.
questions.rationale: One account can guide further inquiry but does not establish prevalence or purchase behavior.

questions.prompt: How should a team recruit a comparable discovery group?
options: Interview anyone available and combine all answers.
Recruit only people who praise the idea.
Choose a group based on assumed spending power alone.
Define a relevant shared situation and record why each person qualifies.
questions.correct_answer: Define a relevant shared situation and record why each person qualifies.
questions.rationale: A stated segment criterion makes cases more comparable and recruitment assumptions visible.

questions.prompt: A customer calls a task 'a nightmare.' Which follow-up is most informative?
options: Would our app fix it?
Can we quote you saying that?
What happened the last time you did it?
So everyone finds this impossible?
questions.correct_answer: What happened the last time you did it?
questions.rationale: Asking for a recent instance reveals the steps and consequences behind a broad label.

questions.prompt: The founder suspects unclear instructions cause missed steps. How should notes separate evidence from theory?
options: Treat the founder's explanation as the interview result.
Record the observed pause and question, then label unclear wording as a possible cause.
Write that instructions are confusing as a proven fact.
Record only that customers dislike the product.
questions.correct_answer: Record the observed pause and question, then label unclear wording as a possible cause.
questions.rationale: Separating behavior from its possible cause keeps the causal claim testable.

questions.prompt: Which practice respects a discovery participant? In this case, the team is working after a schedule change; keep that constraint in view.
options: Explain the purpose, ask permission to take notes, and allow questions to be skipped.
Hide that the conversation is research.
Promise a benefit for favorable answers.
Collect irrelevant identifying details just in case.
questions.correct_answer: Explain the purpose, ask permission to take notes, and allow questions to be skipped.
questions.rationale: Purpose, consent, and the ability to decline support participant autonomy and trust.

questions.prompt: Interview accounts disagree about how often an issue occurs. What is a sound next step?
options: Treat the most vivid quote as a representative count.
Adopt the founder's preferred estimate.
Stop recording contradictory accounts.
Write a frequency hypothesis and seek evidence that could support or weaken it.
questions.correct_answer: Write a frequency hypothesis and seek evidence that could support or weaken it.
questions.rationale: Explicitly tracking uncertainty prevents anecdotes from being mistaken for frequency evidence.

questions.prompt: How should a team investigate an existing workaround?
options: Ignore it because it is not another company.
Ask whether the team's design is better.
Ask about its effort, tradeoffs, and use in a recent case.
Assume workaround users will adopt a new product.
questions.correct_answer: Ask about its effort, tradeoffs, and use in a recent case.
questions.rationale: Workarounds are alternatives; their actual costs help explain customer choices.

questions.prompt: When should a discovery team continue research? In this case, the team is working after a schedule change; keep that constraint in view.
options: Only after the product has launched.
When a clear, material uncertainty remains and there is a practical way to examine it.
Whenever interviewees compliment the founder.
Until every interviewee agrees.
questions.correct_answer: When a clear, material uncertainty remains and there is a practical way to examine it.
questions.rationale: Research is useful when it addresses a defined uncertainty, not when it merely collects praise.

questions.prompt: What makes a problem claim usefully falsifiable? In this case, the team is working when information arrives on paper; keep that constraint in view.

Remove all boundaries from the statement.

questions.prompt: Two causes could explain a delay. What should happen before choosing a solution?

Gather evidence that can distinguish the competing explanations.
Choose the cheapest feature and declare success.
Treat both causes as confirmed.
questions.correct_answer: Gather evidence that can distinguish the competing explanations.
questions.rationale: Different causes call for different responses, so discriminating evidence matters.

questions.prompt: How can the team express uncertainty honestly? In this case, the team is working when information arrives on paper; keep that constraint in view.
options: Accounts suggest this obstacle in cases heard; its frequency and cause remain unverified.
All customers have this issue.
Our concept has already solved it.
No further evidence is needed.
questions.correct_answer: Accounts suggest this obstacle in cases heard; its frequency and cause remain unverified.
questions.rationale: This phrasing reports the scope of evidence and states what is not yet known.

learning_objectives: Apply funding, pivots, and resilience principles to the Sanaa Photo Walks case.
Distinguish observed information from an unverified assumption.
Choose a proportionate next action and explain its tradeoffs.

questions.prompt: What comparison best covers self-funding and outside capital?
options: Investor title alone.
Control, repayment or ownership, timing, reporting, and fit with a milestone.
Headline amount alone.
A claim one source always succeeds.
questions.correct_answer: Control, repayment or ownership, timing, reporting, and fit with a milestone.
questions.rationale: Funding choices carry governance and financial effects beyond the amount.

questions.prompt: Debt has a fixed repayment schedule while revenue is uncertain. What should be assessed?
options: Ability to pay under cautious cash scenarios and consequences of shortfalls.
Whether debt removes risk.
Product appearance.
Whether future revenue can be guaranteed.
questions.correct_answer: Ability to pay under cautious cash scenarios and consequences of shortfalls.
questions.rationale: Repayment remains an obligation when receipts are delayed or weaker.

questions.prompt: What should founders examine in an equity offer? In this case, the team is working when information arrives on paper; keep that constraint in view.
options: Cash received with no ownership effect.
A guarantee of growth.
A promise founders retain sole control.
Capital and potential support against dilution, governance, and expectation alignment.
questions.correct_answer: Capital and potential support against dilution, governance, and expectation alignment.
questions.rationale: Equity changes ownership and may affect governance as well as adding resources.

questions.prompt: A grant is restricted to one activity. What must be checked?
options: That grants have no conditions.
That funds arrive immediately.
Eligibility, permitted use, conditions, reporting, timing, and plan-change rules.
Only the advertised maximum.
questions.correct_answer: Eligibility, permitted use, conditions, reporting, timing, and plan-change rules.
questions.rationale: Restrictions and timing must match the venture's project and compliance capacity.

questions.prompt: The venture's cash runway is narrowing. What is responsible?
options: Assume new funding is certain.
Update cash assumptions and commitments and compare options before urgency.
Ignore payment dates.
Use only optimistic sales.
questions.correct_answer: Update cash assumptions and commitments and compare options before urgency.
questions.rationale: A candid cash view preserves choices better than waiting for a shortfall.

questions.prompt: A pilot challenges the current assumption, while another group reports a different need. What is a pivot?
options: A material change such as segment or offer, based on evidence and tested as a new hypothesis.
Renaming without changing assumptions.
Hiding pilot results.
Declaring success before retesting.
questions.correct_answer: A material change such as segment or offer, based on evidence and tested as a new hypothesis.
questions.rationale: A pivot changes a meaningful strategic hypothesis and needs subsequent validation.

questions.prompt: When can persistence be more reasonable than pivoting? In this case, the team is working when information arrives on paper; keep that constraint in view.
options: Whenever the founder dislikes criticism.
When no evidence exists.
Whenever sunk cost is high.
When evidence still supports the problem and a testable execution issue remains.
questions.correct_answer: When evidence still supports the problem and a testable execution issue remains.
questions.rationale: Persistence can fit when the premise remains supported and execution uncertainty can be tested.

questions.prompt: After a setback, what is a prudent response to pressure to spend personal funds?
options: Promise a recovery date without evidence.
Conceal the setback from affected parties.
Pause, review obligations and options with trusted qualified support, and avoid unsupported commitments.
Borrow at any terms to prove commitment.
questions.correct_answer: Pause, review obligations and options with trusted qualified support, and avoid unsupported commitments.
questions.rationale: A deliberate review avoids pressured choices based on false certainty.

questions.prompt: How should a forecast be presented to a prospective funder?
options: Use unsupported statistics.
Show assumptions, scenarios, evidence status, risks, and what could change it.
Present one precise projection as guaranteed.
Remove downside cases.
questions.correct_answer: Show assumptions, scenarios, evidence status, risks, and what could change it.
questions.rationale: Transparent assumptions make a forecast interpretable without making a promise.

questions.prompt: Funding terms require rapid growth that may reduce quality. What should the team do? In this case, the team is working when information arrives on paper; keep that constraint in view.
options: Assess strategic fit, operational capacity, safeguards, and consequences before accepting.
Accept because capital always helps.
Assume quality can be repaired at no cost.
Ignore attached conditions.
questions.correct_answer: Assess strategic fit, operational capacity, safeguards, and consequences before accepting.
questions.rationale: Terms can shape pace; the team should assess whether it can meet them responsibly.

options: Eligibility, permitted use, conditions, reporting, timing, and plan-change rules.
Only the advertised maximum.
That grants have no conditions.
That funds arrive immediately.
questions.correct_answer: Eligibility, permitted use, conditions, reporting, timing, and plan-change rules.
questions.rationale: Restrictions and timing must match the venture's project and compliance capacity.

questions.prompt: The venture's cash runway is narrowing. What is responsible?
options: Ignore payment dates.
Use only optimistic sales.
Assume new funding is certain.
Update cash assumptions and commitments and compare options before urgency.
questions.correct_answer: Update cash assumptions and commitments and compare options before urgency.
questions.rationale: A candid cash view preserves choices better than waiting for a shortfall.

questions.prompt: A pilot challenges the current assumption, while another group reports a different need. What is a pivot?
options: Hiding pilot results.
Declaring success before retesting.
A material change such as segment or offer, based on evidence and tested as a new hypothesis.
Renaming without changing assumptions.
questions.correct_answer: A material change such as segment or offer, based on evidence and tested as a new hypothesis.
questions.rationale: A pivot changes a meaningful strategic hypothesis and needs subsequent validation.

questions.prompt: When can persistence be more reasonable than pivoting? In this case, the team is working during a short pilot; keep that constraint in view.
options: Whenever sunk cost is high.
When evidence still supports the problem and a testable execution issue remains.
Whenever the founder dislikes criticism.
When no evidence exists.
questions.correct_answer: When evidence still supports the problem and a testable execution issue remains.
questions.rationale: Persistence can fit when the premise remains supported and execution uncertainty can be tested.

questions.prompt: After a setback, what is a prudent response to pressure to spend personal funds?
options: Pause, review obligations and options with trusted qualified support, and avoid unsupported commitments.
Borrow at any terms to prove commitment.
Promise a recovery date without evidence.
Conceal the setback from affected parties.
questions.correct_answer: Pause, review obligations and options with trusted qualified support, and avoid unsupported commitments.
questions.rationale: A deliberate review avoids pressured choices based on false certainty.

questions.prompt: How should a forecast be presented to a prospective funder?
options: Present one precise projection as guaranteed.
Remove downside cases.
Use unsupported statistics.
Show assumptions, scenarios, evidence status, risks, and what could change it.
questions.correct_answer: Show assumptions, scenarios, evidence status, risks, and what could change it.
questions.rationale: Transparent assumptions make a forecast interpretable without making a promise.

questions.prompt: Funding terms require rapid growth that may reduce quality. What should the team do? In this case, the team is working during a short pilot; keep that constraint in view.
options: Assume quality can be repaired at no cost.
Ignore attached conditions.
Assess strategic fit, operational capacity, safeguards, and consequences before accepting.
Accept because capital always helps.
questions.correct_answer: Assess strategic fit, operational capacity, safeguards, and consequences before accepting.
questions.rationale: Terms can shape pace; the team should assess whether it can meet them responsibly.
